segments.voice: Yesterday, reading the Gita's first chapter: samavetan, the gathered ones, and a list where every name was family. Now Arjuna says what seeing them does to him.

Before a big moment a body can take over: a dry mouth, shaky hands, knees that won't hold still. One question for today: can a sacred text let someone fall apart, out loud, on the page? The Gita's first chapter answers in Arjuna's own voice. So far he's been seen from outside. He raised his bow. He spoke to Krishna. He looked. Then he describes himself, and the small words change to mama and me: my.
screen: `DRY MOUTH, SHAKY HANDS.` → `CAN A SACRED TEXT LET SOMEONE FALL APART?` → `MAMA, ME: MY.`

segments.voice: Sanjaya sets it up: pity, kripa, took him over, and he spoke. Then Arjuna: drishtvemam svajanam krishna yuyutsum samupasthitam. Having seen my own people, Krishna, standing near, eager to fight. Drishtvemam is drishtva and imam melted together: having seen these. And svajanam, my own people, the word from last week. And yuyutsum, wanting to fight, is the word from the very first line, now said about his own family. Then the body. Sidanti mama gatrani: my limbs sink. Mukham cha parishushyati: and my mouth goes dry. Gandivam sramsate hastat: Gandiva, the bow, slips from my hand. He doesn't throw it. The verb belongs to the bow: it slips. And the Gita doesn't cut him off; he speaks in full before Krishna answers. A neighbor tradition keeps words like these too. In the Psalms, kept by Jews and Christians, a voice says: "I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint: my heart is like wax." What's shared: a sacred book that lets a body's collapse be said plainly, in the first person. One honest difference: the Psalm is spoken to God, a prayer from inside the trouble. Arjuna speaks to Krishna, here still his charioteer and friend, and he's making a case not to fight. Krishna's reply, in chapter two, will push back.
screen: `KRIPA: PITY TAKES HIM OVER.` · `MY LIMBS SINK. MY MOUTH GOES DRY.` · `THE BOW SLIPS.` · `A PSALM: POURED OUT LIKE WATER.` · then, large: `THE BATTLE MOVES INTO A BODY.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes if you like, and move your attention slowly from your feet to your hands, your mouth, your breath, naming each place silently as you reach it. Where anything feels tight or dry or shaky, leave it be, and simply know it's there. If closing your eyes isn't comfortable, lower your gaze to the floor.
Reading the Gita's first chapter: today, mama and me, my, the small words that turn the story inward, toward a body on a chariot: my limbs, my mouth, my hand.
Your line: reading the Gita's first chapter in the original. Here the battle moves into a body. That's today's reading.

howItsDone: Some Hindus read the Gita in order, a chapter at a time, so Arjuna's distress in chapter one is heard in full before Krishna's reply begins in chapter two.
